solution:
A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its modes satisfy \( L = (2p-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} \) with \( p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \), i.e. only ODD harmonics are present.

Count the nodes mode by mode, taking the closed end at \( x = 0 \):

| mode | \( L \) | nodes in the pipe | frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| fundamental | \( \lambda/4 \) | 1 (at the closed end) | \( n \) |
| next | \( 3\lambda/4 \) | 2 | \( 3n \) |
| next | \( 5\lambda/4 \) | 3 | \( 5n \) |

For the third mode \( \lambda = \dfrac{4L}{5} \), and the displacement nodes lie at \( x = 0,\ \dfrac{2L}{5},\ \dfrac{4L}{5} \) — exactly THREE nodes, the next one at \( \dfrac{6L}{5} \) falling outside the pipe.

So three nodes corresponds to the fifth harmonic, whose frequency is \( 5 \) times the fundamental.

Discrimination: (A) 2 and (C) 4 are even multiples, which a closed pipe cannot produce at all; (B) 3 is the mode with only TWO nodes. Only (D) survives.

\( \therefore \) the frequency is \( 5 \) times the fundamental frequency — option (D).

For a pipe open at both ends the fundamental frequency is \( n = \dfrac{v}{2l} \) (end correction neglected).

With \( l_1 = 0.50 \) m and \( l_2 = 0.51 \) m,
\( n_1 = \dfrac{v}{2(0.50)} = \dfrac{v}{1.00} \) and \( n_2 = \dfrac{v}{2(0.51)} = \dfrac{v}{1.02} \).

The shorter pipe has the higher frequency, so the beat frequency is
\( \Delta n = n_1 - n_2 = v\left( \dfrac{1}{1.00} - \dfrac{1}{1.02} \right) = v \times \dfrac{0.02}{1.02} \).

Setting \( \Delta n = 7 \) Hz:
\( v = \dfrac{7 \times 1.02}{0.02} = 7 \times 51 = 357 \) m/s.

Discrimination — the beat frequency each option would give is \( v \times \dfrac{0.02}{1.02} \):
(A) 307 m/s \( \to 6.02 \) Hz, (B) 327 m/s \( \to 6.41 \) Hz, (C) 350 m/s \( \to 6.86 \) Hz, (D) 357 m/s \( \to 7.00 \) Hz. Only (D) gives exactly 7 beats per second.

\( \therefore \) the speed of sound is \( 357 \) m/s — option (D).

By the law of tension, the fundamental frequency of a stretched wire is \( n = \dfrac{1}{2l}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}} \), so with the vibrating length and the linear density unchanged \( n \propto \sqrt{T} \).

The tension is increased by 25%, so \( T' = 1.25\,T \), and
\( \dfrac{n'}{n} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T'}{T}} = \sqrt{1.25} = 1.118 \approx 1.12 \).

Discrimination: (A) 0.8 is a DECREASE, whereas raising the tension must raise the frequency; (C) 1.25 is the tension ratio itself, which would require \( n \propto T \); (D) 1.56 is \( (1.25)^2 \). Only (B) equals \( \sqrt{1.25} \).

\( \therefore \) the frequency becomes \( 1.12 \) times the original — option (B).

A progressive (travelling) wave must have its phase in the combined form \( (kq \mp \omega t) \), where \( q \) is the coordinate ALONG WHICH the wave travels. For travel along the \( y \)-axis the phase must therefore contain \( ky \) together with \( \omega t \) inside a single sine or cosine.

Option (A) \( x = A \sin(ky - \omega t) \): the phase is \( ky - \omega t \), so a point of constant phase moves with \( y = \dfrac{\omega}{k}t + \) constant — the wave advances along \( +y \). The displacement \( x \) is perpendicular to \( y \), so this is a transverse wave travelling along the \( y \)-axis.

Discrimination:
- (B) \( y = A \sin(kx - \omega t) \) — the phase depends on \( x \), so this wave travels along the \( x \)-axis, not the \( y \)-axis.
- (C) \( y = A \sin(ky)\cos(\omega t) \) and (D) \( y = A \cos(ky)\sin(\omega t) \) — in both, the space and time terms are SEPARATE factors. That is the form of a stationary wave (compare Eq. 6.12 of this chapter, \( y = 2a\cos\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\sin 2\pi nt \)): the profile does not advance, it only changes amplitude in place, and it has permanent nodes. Neither represents a travelling wave.

\( \therefore \) option (A) represents a wave travelling along the \( y \)-axis.

At a FIXED end the string cannot move, so a node forms there. At a FREE end the string is completely free to move, so an antinode forms there.

The distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is \( \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \), and successive nodes and antinodes then alternate every \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \). Hence the possible lengths are
\( L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4},\ \dfrac{3\lambda}{4},\ \dfrac{5\lambda}{4},\ \ldots \)
i.e. \( L = (2p-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} \), \( p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \) — an ODD integral multiple of \( \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \).

Discrimination: an odd multiple of \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \) (B), an odd multiple of \( \lambda \) (C) and an even multiple of \( \lambda \) (D) are all integral multiples of \( \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \), and every such length puts the SAME kind of point (node or antinode) at both ends. None of them can place a node at one end and an antinode at the other.

\( \therefore \) the length must be an odd integral multiple of \( \dfrac{\lambda}{4} \) — option (A).
